## In 60 seconds

An electrogram on a mapping screen has passed through a chain: amplifier, analog filters, a converter that samples
and quantizes, then digital filters. Every stage changes what you can measure. **Sampling** at $f_s$ cannot
distinguish frequencies above $f_s/2$ from lower ones (aliasing), so they must be removed first, and it limits timing
to about a sample unless you interpolate. **Quantization** adds noise of one step over $\sqrt{12}$, which sets a ceiling
of about 6 dB per bit. **Filters** remove what you do not want, mains interference, baseline wander, far-field
activity, but also reshape what you do want: a high-pass removes the slow components of a unipolar signal, and a
causal filter shifts features in time by its group delay. Clinical recordings use different bands for unipolar and
bipolar signals; the same electrogram looks different in each, and its activation time can move.

## From the field

- **Bands differ by signal type.** One clinical mapping study recorded minimally filtered unipolar electrograms at
  0.5–500 Hz, high-pass filtered unipolar electrograms at 100 Hz and bipolar electrograms at 30–500 Hz, at 205 sites in
  40 patients with focal tachycardias [@delacretaz2001]. Demo m04-d2 applies these bands to a model unipolar signal.
- **High-pass filtering trades far field for morphology.** It can reduce the far-field part of a unipolar signal but
  limits what can be inferred from the electrogram's shape [@stevenson2005]. Lab part D shows both effects.
- **Using both signals together.** In the same study, the interval from the onset of the minimally filtered unipolar
  signal to the first peak of the bipolar signal correlated with timing against the surface ECG (r = 0.85), and was
  shorter at sites where ablation succeeded than where it did not (3.8 ± 3.5 versus 9.2 ± 5.2 ms) [@delacretaz2001].
  The filter settings are part of that measurement.
- **Know the converter.** The PhysioNet Intracardiac Atrial Fibrillation Database used in m03 and m31 was sampled at
  1 kHz with 14-bit resolution [@iafdb]. At 1 kHz a sharp activation can only be timed to about 0.3 ms without
  interpolation (lab part A).

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $f$ frequency (Hz). $f_s$ sampling rate (Hz), $T = 1/f_s$ sampling interval. $N$ number
of bits. $V_{FS}$ full-scale voltage, $q = 2V_{FS}/2^N$ the quantization step (LSB). $f_c$ filter cutoff (Hz), $n$
filter order. $H(f)$ frequency response. $f_0$ notch frequency, $Q$ quality factor. Signals in relative units.

### Sampling

Sampling keeps $x[n] = x(nT)$. A sinusoid at $f$ and one at $f$ shifted by any multiple of $f_s$ give identical
samples, so every frequency folds into $[0, f_s/2]$:

$$
f_{\text{alias}} = \left\lvert f - f_s\,\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{f}{f_s}\right)\right\rvert
$$ {#eq-m04-sampling}

Anything above the **Nyquist frequency** $f_s/2$ must be removed by an analog low-pass filter before the converter; no
later processing can separate it from real low-frequency content. Sampling also limits timing: locating the steepest
downstroke (the m03 activation marker) at the nearest sample has an error spread of $T/\sqrt{12}$, about 0.29 ms at
1 kHz; fitting a parabola through the slope around its minimum cuts that by more than an order of magnitude for a
smooth signal (lab part A).

::: {.demo #m04-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m04-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m04-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m04-d1-aliasing.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m04-sampling for an ideal sampler and a pure cosine; the alias drawn is the lowest-frequency cosine
  through the same samples. Tested against `epml.recording`.
- Parameters: signal 5–1500 Hz and sampling rate 100–2000 Hz, free choices for illustration.
- What it ignores: the anti-aliasing filter, converter noise and clock jitter.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Frequencies above $f_s/2$ fold down and cannot be removed afterwards.
- Timing at the nearest sample is uncertain by about $T/\sqrt{12}$; interpolation helps.

### Quantization

An $N$-bit converter spanning $\pm V_{FS}$ rounds to steps of $q = 2V_{FS}/2^N$. If the error is spread evenly over one
step, its variance is $q^2/12$. For a full-scale sine of amplitude $V_{FS}$, the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio is

$$
\mathrm{SQNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{V_{FS}^2/2}{q^2/12} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(2^N\sqrt{3/2}\right) \approx 6.02N + 1.76\ \text{dB}
$$ {#eq-m04-quantization}

A 14-bit converter gives about 86 dB for a full-scale sine. A signal that uses a fraction of the range loses 6 dB for
every halving of its amplitude, so gain before the converter matters.

**Key takeaways**

- Quantization noise is one step over $\sqrt{12}$.
- About 6 dB per bit for a full-scale signal; less for small signals.

### Filters

A first-order RC high-pass has

$$
H(f) = \frac{jf/f_c}{1 + jf/f_c}
$$ {#eq-m04-highpass}

At $f_c$ it passes $1/\sqrt2$ of the amplitude with a 45° phase lead; far below $f_c$, $H \approx jf/f_c$, a scaled
differentiator. Butterworth filters are maximally flat in the passband:

$$
\lvert H(f)\rvert^2 = \frac{1}{1 + (f/f_c)^{2n}}
$$ {#eq-m04-butterworth}

for a low-pass of order $n$ (replace $f/f_c$ by $f_c/f$ for a high-pass). Digital versions come from the bilinear
transform with the cutoff prewarped, which keeps the −3 dB point exactly at $f_c$; the lab builds first- and
second-order sections by hand and checks them against scipy.

**Delay.** A causal filter delays slowly varying features by its group delay. For analog Butterworth low-passes, at
low frequencies,

$$
\tau_g = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c}\ (n = 1), \qquad \tau_g = \frac{\sqrt2}{2\pi f_c}\ (n = 2)
$$ {#eq-m04-delay}

so a second-order 100 Hz low-pass delays a 10-ms bump by about 2.3 ms. Filtering forward and then backward cancels
the phase (zero phase) and squares the magnitude, but needs the whole record, so it is for offline analysis. A
linear-phase FIR filter delays every frequency equally ([eq-m34-fir-delay](m34-software-architecture.qmd#eq-m34-fir-delay)).

**Mains interference.** A second-order notch at $f_0$ with quality factor $Q$,

$$
H(z) = g\,\frac{1 - 2\cos\omega_0\,z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{1 - 2g\cos\omega_0\,z^{-1} + (2g - 1)\,z^{-2}}, \qquad
\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi f_0}{f_s}, \qquad g = \frac{1}{1 + \tan(\omega_0/2Q)}
$$ {#eq-m04-notch}

removes $f_0$ exactly, passes DC and the Nyquist frequency unchanged, and has a −3 dB bandwidth of $f_0/Q$. A narrow
notch (large $Q$) barely touches the electrogram but rings longer.

::: {.demo #m04-d2 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m04-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m04-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m04-d2-filter-egm.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the m03 unipolar electrogram ([eq-m03-unipolar-closed](m03-electrograms.qmd#eq-m03-unipolar-closed)),
  a simplified model, computed at 20 kHz and passed through second-order Butterworth high-pass and low-pass
  filters (@eq-m04-butterworth), causally or forward and backward. Tested against `epml.recording`.
- Parameters: front at 1 m/s, width 0.3 mm, electrode 1 mm away (m03 defaults); band presets from one clinical study
  [@delacretaz2001]; other cutoffs are free choices.
- What it ignores: amplifier noise and gain, the analog anti-aliasing filter, sampling and quantization, filter order
  and type used by any particular system, and real electrogram shapes.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A high-pass removes slow components and changes shape; it lowers peak-to-peak amplitude.
- Causal filters shift features in time; zero-phase filtering does not, but only offline.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Every displayed electrogram, voltage and activation time depends on the recording
chain. Reviews of recording technique note that high-pass filtering and digital sampling both influence electrogram
characteristics [@stevenson2005]. One study used minimally filtered unipolar (0.5–500 Hz), high-pass filtered unipolar
(100 Hz) and bipolar (30–500 Hz) recordings from the same catheter to judge local prematurity during mapping of focal
tachycardias [@delacretaz2001].

**What the evidence is.** A review [@stevenson2005] and one clinical study of 40 patients and 205 mapping sites
[@delacretaz2001]. Filter settings, sampling rates and resolutions vary between systems; numbers here describe the
cited studies and our own models, not any system's defaults.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **What band and filter type were used?** They set shape, amplitude and timing (@eq-m04-butterworth, @eq-m04-delay).
- **Was filtering causal or zero-phase?** Live annotation sees the delay (@eq-m04-delay).
- **What were the sampling rate and resolution?** They limit timing and small-signal fidelity
  (@eq-m04-sampling, @eq-m04-quantization).

## How experts think

When an electrogram or a measurement looks wrong, walk the chain:

1. **Is anything aliased?** Was there an anti-aliasing filter below $f_s/2$ (@eq-m04-sampling)?
2. **Is the signal using the converter's range?** Small signals lose 6 dB per halving (@eq-m04-quantization).
3. **What band was applied?** High-pass reshapes and shrinks; low-pass smooths and delays (@eq-m04-butterworth).
4. **Causal or zero-phase?** Live timing includes the group delay (@eq-m04-delay).
5. **Is there mains interference, and how was it removed?** A notch is narrow but rings (@eq-m04-notch).

One sentence to keep: **the electrogram on the screen is the tissue signal times the chain's transfer function;
know the chain before you trust the shape or the timing.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Aliasing (@eq-m04-sampling) | $f_{\text{alias}} = \lvert f - f_s\,\mathrm{round}(f/f_s)\rvert$; remove content above $f_s/2$ before sampling |
| Timing at the nearest sample | error spread $T/\sqrt{12}$ (0.29 ms at 1 kHz) |
| Quantization (@eq-m04-quantization) | noise $q/\sqrt{12}$; SQNR $\approx 6.02N + 1.76$ dB for a full-scale sine |
| RC high-pass (@eq-m04-highpass) | $1/\sqrt2$ and +45° at $f_c$; differentiator far below $f_c$ |
| Butterworth (@eq-m04-butterworth) | $\lvert H\rvert^2 = 1/(1 + (f/f_c)^{2n})$ |
| Group delay (@eq-m04-delay) | $1/(2\pi f_c)$ (order 1), $\sqrt2/(2\pi f_c)$ (order 2); zero phase removes it offline |
| Notch (@eq-m04-notch) | zero at $f_0$; −3 dB bandwidth $f_0/Q$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Unipolar 0.5–500 Hz, high-pass unipolar 100 Hz, bipolar 30–500 Hz; 205 sites, 40 patients | @delacretaz2001 |
| Unipolar-onset to bipolar-peak interval: r = 0.85 with ECG timing; 3.8 ± 3.5 versus 9.2 ± 5.2 ms | @delacretaz2001 |
| PhysioNet Intracardiac Atrial Fibrillation Database: 1 kHz, 14 bits | @iafdb |
| Timing error, SQNR, filter delays and distortions | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What is aliasing, and why can't you fix it in software?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Content above $f_s/2$ produces the same samples as content at $\lvert f -
f_s\,\mathrm{round}(f/f_s)\rvert$ (@eq-m04-sampling). Once sampled the two are indistinguishable, so it must be filtered out in analog form first.

</details>

**Q2. How precisely can you time an activation sampled at 1 kHz?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

At the nearest sample, with an error spread of about $T/\sqrt{12}$ = 0.29 ms; interpolating the slope around its minimum
does much better for a smooth signal (lab part A).

</details>

**Q3. Derive the 6 dB-per-bit rule.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Uniform rounding error has variance $q^2/12$; a full-scale sine has power $V_{FS}^2/2$ with $q = 2V_{FS}/2^N$, giving
$20\log_{10}(2^N\sqrt{3/2}) \approx 6.02N + 1.76$ dB (@eq-m04-quantization).

</details>

**Q4. Why does a small signal get a worse SQNR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The noise is fixed by the step size, so halving the signal amplitude loses 6 dB (@eq-m04-quantization).

</details>

**Q5. What does a first-order high-pass do at its cutoff and far below it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

At $f_c$, gain $1/\sqrt2$ and a 45° lead; far below, $H \approx jf/f_c$, a scaled differentiator (@eq-m04-highpass).

</details>

**Q6. Why are unipolar and bipolar signals filtered differently?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Bipolar signals are already spatially high-passed (m03), so a 30-Hz high-pass mainly removes baseline drift; unipolar
signals keep far-field and slow components that a high-pass would remove, along with morphology information
[@stevenson2005; @delacretaz2001].

</details>

**Q7. A causal filter moved the activation time. Why, and by how much?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

By its group delay, $\sqrt2/(2\pi f_c)$ for a second-order Butterworth low-pass at low frequencies (@eq-m04-delay),
plus shape changes from the high-pass (lab part D).

</details>

**Q8. When can you use zero-phase filtering?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Offline, when the whole record is available: filtering forward then backward cancels the phase and squares the
magnitude (@eq-m04-delay). Live systems must be causal.

</details>

**Q9. What does a Butterworth filter's order change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The steepness of the transition: $\lvert H\rvert^2 = 1/(1 + (f/f_c)^{2n})$ (@eq-m04-butterworth); higher order also means more
delay and more ringing.

</details>

**Q10. Design a notch for 60 Hz mains. What trade-off do you face?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Bandwidth $f_0/Q$ (@eq-m04-notch): a high $Q$ removes a narrow band and barely changes the electrogram but rings longer
after transients; a low $Q$ settles faster but removes more signal.

</details>

**Q11. Why prewarp the cutoff in the bilinear transform?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The bilinear transform compresses the frequency axis; prewarping places the digital −3 dB point exactly at the
intended $f_c$ (lab part C).

</details>

**Q12. A signal looks clean on one system and fractionated on another. What would you check first?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Band, filter type and order, causal or zero-phase processing, sampling rate and gain: the chain changes shape before
any tissue difference (@eq-m04-butterworth, @eq-m04-sampling; demo m04-d2).

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A 700 Hz sine sampled at 1 kHz appears at what frequency?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

300 Hz (@eq-m04-sampling).

</details>

**S2. You add two bits to a converter. SQNR gain for a full-scale sine?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 12 dB (@eq-m04-quantization).

</details>

**S3. Gain of a first-order high-pass at its cutoff?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1/\sqrt2$, about 0.71 (@eq-m04-highpass).

</details>

**S4. Group delay of a first-order 100 Hz low-pass at low frequencies?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1/(2\pi \cdot 100)$ s, about 1.6 ms (@eq-m04-delay).

</details>

**S5. A 50 Hz notch with Q = 25. Bandwidth?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

2 Hz (@eq-m04-notch).

</details>

**S6. Does zero-phase filtering change amplitude?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Yes: it squares the magnitude response; only the phase is cancelled (@eq-m04-delay).

</details>
